title: Introduction to Acids
content:
# Introduction to Acids

## Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:
- Describe the properties of acids
- Identify common acids and their formulae
- Explain what makes a substance acidic
- State the safety precautions when handling acids

## Introduction

**Acids** are a fundamental class of chemical compounds with characteristic properties. They are found everywhere - in our food (citric acid in lemons), in our bodies (stomach acid), and in industry (sulfuric acid in batteries).

## Key Concepts

### What is an Acid?

**Acid:** A substance that produces hydrogen ions (H⁺) when dissolved in water.

$$\text{HCl(g)} \xrightarrow{\text{water}} \text{H}^+\text{(aq)} + \text{Cl}^-\text{(aq)}$$

**Key point:** It is the **H⁺ ions** (or H₃O⁺, hydronium ions) that give acids their properties.

### Properties of Acids

| Property | Description |
|----------|-------------|
| Taste | Sour (DO NOT taste in lab!) |
| pH | Less than 7 |
| Indicators | Turn litmus red, universal indicator red/orange/yellow |
| Corrosive | Can damage skin, metals, and other materials |
| Conduct electricity | When dissolved (electrolytes) |
| React with | Metals, bases, carbonates |

### Common Acids

**Laboratory acids:**

| Acid | Formula | Found in/used for |
|------|---------|-------------------|
| Hydrochloric acid | HCl | Stomach acid, cleaning |
| Sulfuric acid | H₂SO₄ | Car batteries, industry |
| Nitric acid | HNO₃ | Fertilisers, explosives |

**Everyday acids:**

| Acid | Formula | Found in |
|------|---------|----------|
| Citric acid | C₆H₈O₇ | Citrus fruits |
| Ethanoic acid | CH₃COOH | Vinegar |
| Carbonic acid | H₂CO₃ | Fizzy drinks |
| Lactic acid | C₃H₆O₃ | Sour milk, muscles |
| Ascorbic acid | C₆H₈O₆ | Vitamin C |

### Naming Acids and Their Salts

| Acid | Produces ions | Salt name ending |
|------|---------------|------------------|
| Hydrochloric acid (HCl) | Cl⁻ | -chloride |
| Sulfuric acid (H₂SO₄) | SO₄²⁻ | -sulfate |
| Nitric acid (HNO₃) | NO₃⁻ | -nitrate |
| Phosphoric acid (H₃PO₄) | PO₄³⁻ | -phosphate |
| Ethanoic acid (CH₃COOH) | CH₃COO⁻ | -ethanoate |

### Hydrogen Ions and Acidity

**In solution:**
- Pure acids (not dissolved) don't show acidic properties
- Water is needed to release H⁺ ions
- More H⁺ ions = more acidic = lower pH

**Example:**
- Hydrogen chloride gas (HCl) is not acidic
- When dissolved in water, it ionises: HCl → H⁺ + Cl⁻
- The solution is now acidic

### Concentrated vs Dilute

**Concentrated acid:**
- High proportion of acid to water
- Many H⁺ ions per cm³
- More reactive/dangerous

**Dilute acid:**
- Low proportion of acid to water
- Fewer H⁺ ions per cm³
- Less reactive/dangerous

**Note:** Concentrated and dilute describe amount. Strong and weak describe ionisation (covered later).

### Safety with Acids

**Hazards:**
- Corrosive - can burn skin and eyes
- Harmful if swallowed
- Can damage clothing and surfaces
- React with metals producing flammable hydrogen

**Precautions:**
- Wear safety goggles
- Wear lab coat/apron
- Handle carefully, avoid splashing
- Wash spillages immediately with water
- Work in ventilated area
- Never add water to concentrated acid (always add acid to water)

[DIAGRAM: Hazard symbols - corrosive (two surfaces being corroded), harmful (exclamation mark)]

## Worked Examples

**Example 1:** Write the equation showing how sulfuric acid ionises in water.

**Solution:**
$$\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4\text{(aq)} \rightarrow \text{2H}^+\text{(aq)} + \text{SO}_4^{2-}\text{(aq)}$$

Note: Sulfuric acid produces TWO H⁺ ions per molecule.

---

**Example 2:** Why does dry hydrogen chloride gas not act as an acid?

**Solution:**
- Acids need to release H⁺ ions to show acidic properties
- Dry HCl gas contains covalent molecules
- There are no free H⁺ ions
- Water is needed to ionise the molecules
- Without water, H⁺ ions cannot form
- Therefore, dry HCl doesn't behave as an acid

---

**Example 3:** A student has two solutions - 1M HCl and 0.1M HCl. Which is more acidic? Explain.

**Solution:**
- The 1M HCl is more concentrated
- It contains more H⁺ ions per cm³
- More H⁺ ions means more acidic
- The 1M HCl is more acidic (lower pH)

## Common Mistakes

- **Mistake:** Thinking all acids are dangerous
- **Correct:** Many acids (citric, ethanoic) are safe in dilute form and in food

- **Mistake:** Confusing concentrated with strong
- **Correct:** Concentrated means lots of acid; strong means fully ionised

- **Mistake:** Thinking acids work without water
- **Correct:** Acids need water to release H⁺ ions and show acidic properties

## Practice Questions

1. Define an acid in terms of ions produced. (2 marks)

2. State three properties of acids. (3 marks)

3. Write the formula and name one salt formed by each of these acids:
   a) Hydrochloric acid (2 marks)
   b) Sulfuric acid (2 marks)
   c) Nitric acid (2 marks)

4. Explain why hydrogen chloride gas must be dissolved in water to show acidic properties. (3 marks)

5. A student has concentrated sulfuric acid. State two safety precautions they should take when using it. (2 marks)

6. Explain the difference between a concentrated acid and a dilute acid. (2 marks)

## Key Terms Glossary

| Term | Definition |
|------|------------|
| Acid | A substance that produces H⁺ ions in aqueous solution |
| Hydrogen ion | H⁺, the ion responsible for acidic properties |
| Corrosive | Capable of damaging/destroying materials on contact |
| Concentrated | Contains a high proportion of solute to solvent |
| Dilute | Contains a low proportion of solute to solvent |
| Ionise | To form ions from molecules |

## Summary

- **Acids** produce **H⁺ ions** when dissolved in water
- Common lab acids: HCl, H₂SO₄, HNO₃
- Properties: sour taste, pH < 7, turn litmus red, corrosive
- Acids need **water** to ionise and show acidic properties
- **Concentrated:** lots of acid; **Dilute:** little acid
- Acids react with metals, bases, and carbonates
- Safety: wear goggles, handle carefully, wash spills
